text:
Alex: Heads-up — ran into an odd case with streaming + midflight hedging today. A client observed out-of-order partial chunks after a retry spike.
Maria: Can you paste the minimal repro?
Alex: Sure. Traffic pattern: many 1–2 token responses, intermittent backend slowdowns. Edge hedging enabled (fastfail=60ms, hedge=2). We saw a resume token get applied to a different connection in one path.
Simon: That sounds like a race between resume token assignment and connection swap. Do we still bind tokens to request_id or to connection instance?
Jess: Currently tokens are per-request_id but the proxy assigns the live connection and attaches the latest token when it becomes ready. If a hedge spawns, attach/detach can interleave.
Alex: Right — sequence: primary starts, emits partials, stalls. Hedge kicks, new conn resumes using the latest token, but the primary then flushes buffered partials tagged with the old token. Client reassembles and sees out-of-order chunks.
Maria: Oof. Two problems: ordering guarantees for streaming, and semantics of resume tokens across hedged connections.
Simon: Proposal: treat resume tokens as monotonic offsets (we already do) + enforce single-writer semantics per request_id. That is, only one connection may emit to the client at a time; hedged connections can be ready but must request a handoff and only start emitting after an atomic swap.
Jess: That avoids interleaving but increases tail latency since hedge can’t flush until swap completes. Do we accept that cost?
Alex: Alternative: allow concurrent emit but attach connection-ids to tokens so client fragments include (conn_id, offset) and client reorders. But clients are diverse — we can’t force changes.
Maria: Also impacts billing attribution: if two connections both emit overlapping tokens, we double-bill. We must keep accounting sane.
Simon: Tradeoffs matrix: atomic-swap = preserves order, single-bill, safer for clients. Concurrent-emit = lower latency at risk of ordering and billing complexity.
Jess: Implementation thoughts for atomic-swap: central per-request lock in gateway that coordinates handoff. Handoff sequence: hedge reports Ready(seq_offset), primary requests GraceDrain(timeout), gateway performs swap, drains leftover buffers with sequence-check and then marks new writer.
Alex: Pseudocode sketch I tossed together:
```
// gateway handshake
onNewConnReady(req_id, conn_id, offset) {
  lock(req_id)
  if (current_writer == null || offset > writer_offset + threshold) {
    request_swap(current_writer, conn_id)
    await swap_complete or timeout
    current_writer = conn_id
  }
  unlock(req_id)
}
```
Jess: We also need to cap memory — if writer stalls, hedges shouldn't accumulate unbounded buffers while waiting for swap. Set small per-req buffer cap and fail hedges if exceeded.
Maria: Observability: surface swap events, swap latency, bytes buffered, and any ordering-correctness alerts. Add metric: swap_failures_per_minute.
Simon: Edge cases: what about proxies that crash mid-swap? Need idempotent swap protocol and resume token durability in the control-plane store (etcd-like). Ensure leases so stale writers can be revoked.
Alex: Also consider a "grace window" config per route: how long to wait for primary to drain vs give new writer immediate cutover. For low-latency routes, set window=10ms; for high-reliability routes, window=200ms.
Jess: That would let product teams choose ordering vs latency tradeoffs per route. Good.
Maria: Action items: 1) Prototype per-request lock + swap handshake (Simon) 2) Add router config for grace_window and buffer_cap (Jess) 3) Add metrics + tracing for swaps (Maria) 4) Run perf tests with 10k req/s small-chunk workload (Alex)
Simon: I'll start a spike branch. Question: do we need client-facing change? Ideally no. Keep resume token semantics identical: internal only.
Alex: Agreed. If we must change client protocol, it's a long migration.
Jess: FYI infra-bot: rolling canary for this change will need a paired control-plane migration for the swap lease table.
infra-bot: @channel Reminder: file an infra RFC for control-plane migration steps and rollback plan. See https://redwood-internal/infra/rfcs for template. :robot_face:
Maria: One more note — add a unit test that simulates primary flush after swap to assert no out-of-order delivery. Low-fi test harness is fine.
Alex: Cool. I'll log the incident link and attach the sample trace. For now, mark the thread as "followup: swap-probe" in my notes.
Simon: Thanks — posting PR link when spike lands.
Jess: :thumbsup:
Maria: lgtm.
